questions.question: 1. Quick Sort is generally considered to be:

answers.a: A stable sorting algorithm in every implementation
answers.b: An unstable sorting algorithm in every implementation
answers.c: Stable only when the input array is already sorted
answers.d: Dependent on the implementation; the standard in-place version is generally not stable

explanations.a: Incorrect. Quick Sort does not preserve the relative order of equal elements in every implementation.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Stability can depend on how the algorithm is implemented.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Whether the input is already sorted does not by itself determine stability.
explanations.d: Correct. Standard in-place Quick Sort is generally not stable, although a specially designed implementation can preserve stability.

questions.question: 2. Given a random policy for choosing the pivot, when can Quick Sort encounter its worst-case time complexity?

answers.a: When most chosen pivots are the smallest elements in their respective subarrays
answers.b: When most chosen pivots are the largest elements in their respective subarrays
answers.c: When most pivots divide their subarrays into two approximately equal parts
answers.d: When either a or b occurs repeatedly

explanations.a: Incorrect. Repeatedly selecting the smallest element creates highly unbalanced partitions, but this is only one of the two extreme patterns described.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Repeatedly selecting the largest element also creates highly unbalanced partitions, but this is only one of the two extreme patterns described.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Approximately equal partitions produce a balanced recursion pattern rather than the worst-case pattern.
explanations.d: Correct. Repeatedly choosing either the smallest or the largest element leaves one partition nearly empty and the other almost unchanged, producing the worst-case $O(n^2)$ time complexity.

questions.question:
3. Consider the following Quick Sort pseudo-code. Which pair can be selected for blanks (A) and (B) simultaneously so that values smaller than the pivot go to smaller_array and values greater than or equal to the pivot go to bigger_array?
quick_sort(array) -> sorted-array:
    if array is empty: return array
    pivot = choose_pivot_index()
    smaller_array = [], bigger_array = []
    for i = 1 to sizeof(array):
        if (-----A-----):
            append array[i] to smaller_array
        else if (-----B-----):
            append array[i] to bigger_array
    return quick_sort(smaller_array) + [array[pivot]] + quick_sort(bigger_array)

explanations.a: Correct. The first condition sends values strictly smaller than the pivot to smaller_array, while the second condition sends values greater than or equal to the pivot to bigger_array.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This pair assigns values equal to the pivot to the first condition rather than to the stated bigger partition.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Values equal to the pivot satisfy neither condition, so the pair does not cover all possible values.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Values equal to the pivot satisfy the first condition, so they are not handled according to the stated partitioning rule.

questions.question: 4. What is the average-case time complexity of Quick Sort when pivot selection produces reasonably balanced partitions?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Quadratic time occurs in the worst case when partitions are repeatedly highly unbalanced.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A linear bound is too small because each level of partitioning processes elements and there are multiple levels.
explanations.c: Correct. Reasonably balanced partitions give approximately $\log_2(n)$ recursion levels, with about $O(n)$ partitioning work at each level, resulting in $O(n \log n)$ average-case time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The recursion depth can be logarithmic for balanced partitions, but the partitioning work at each level also contributes to the total running time.

questions.question: 5. What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort when every partition places only one element on one side of the pivot and all remaining elements on the other side?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The algorithm still performs partitioning work across many recursive levels.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This complexity corresponds to balanced partitioning rather than repeatedly unbalanced partitioning.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Although recursion depth is related to the number of levels, the total partitioning work is not logarithmic in this case.
explanations.d: Correct. With one highly unbalanced partition at every level, the work is approximately $n + (n-1) + (n-2) + \cdots + 1$, which is $O(n^2)$.

questions.question: 6. Which statement best describes the auxiliary space complexity of recursive Quick Sort?

answers.a: It is always $O(1)$ regardless of pivot selection.
answers.b: It is typically $O(\log n)$ for balanced recursion but can become $O(n)$ in the worst case.
answers.c: It is always $O(n^2)$ because every partition creates a new array.
answers.d: It is always $O(n)$ because Quick Sort stores a complete copy of the input.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Recursive calls require stack space, and the number of active calls depends on the partition balance.
explanations.b: Correct. Balanced recursive partitions produce logarithmic recursion depth, while highly unbalanced partitions can produce linear recursion depth.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Recursive Quick Sort does not inherently require quadratic auxiliary storage.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A standard in-place implementation does not need to store a complete copy of the input array.

questions.question: 7. Which property of Quick Sort is most directly responsible for its average-case time complexity of $O(n \log n)$?

answers.a: The array is divided into approximately equal subarrays over successive partitioning steps.
answers.b: Every element is compared with every other element exactly once.
answers.c: The algorithm always chooses the smallest element as the pivot.
answers.d: The algorithm performs no comparisons after the first partition.

explanations.a: Correct. When partitions are reasonably balanced, the recursion has about $\log_2(n)$ levels and each level performs a total of approximately $O(n)$ partitioning work.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Comparing every pair of elements would lead to substantially more work than the average behavior of Quick Sort.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Consistently choosing the smallest element creates highly unbalanced partitions.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Quick Sort continues partitioning its subarrays recursively after the first partition.

questions.question: 8. If the pivot divides an array of size $n$ into two subarrays of approximately equal size, which recurrence best represents the running time of Quick Sort for that partition pattern?

explanations.a: Incorrect. This represents a highly unbalanced recursion pattern with only one subproblem of size close to $n$.
explanations.b: Correct. Two approximately half-sized subarrays are processed recursively, and partitioning the current array requires linear work, giving $T(n) = 2T(n / 2) + O(n)$.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The balanced partition produces two recursive subproblems rather than one.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The recursive subproblems are smaller than the original array; the recurrence does not contain two calls on size $n$.

questions.question: 9. Which comparison of sorting algorithms is correct for their typical time complexities?

answers.a: Quick Sort has $O(n \log n)$ average-case time, while Merge Sort has $O(n \log n)$ worst-case time.
answers.b: Quick Sort has $O(n)$ worst-case time, while Bubble Sort has $O(\log n)$ worst-case time.
answers.c: Quick Sort has $O(\log n)$ average-case time, while Heap Sort has $O(n)$ worst-case time.
answers.d: Quick Sort has $O(n^2)$ average-case time, while Merge Sort has $O(n^2)$ worst-case time.

explanations.a: Correct. With reasonably balanced partitions, Quick Sort has average-case time $O(n \log n)$, while Merge Sort has worst-case time $O(n \log n)$.
explanations.b: Incorrect. The stated worst-case complexities are too low for both algorithms.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Sorting the input requires processing its elements, so these logarithmic and linear bounds do not describe the stated average and worst cases.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The stated quadratic average-case complexity for Quick Sort and quadratic worst-case complexity for Merge Sort do not match their standard time-complexity analysis.
